newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Archaeologists keep the pace set by Indiana Jones.
newsitem.headline: Archaeologists keep the pace set by Indiana Jones.

text.p: The Hollywood movies about archaeologist Indiana Jones took the box office by storm with their death-defying adventures of the whip-cracking scientist as he chased ancient treasures.
But it seems that that is what life out in the field can really be like.
The stories of two Australian archaeologists who cheated death -- one from deadly mosquitoes and another after jumping half naked into a raging river -- have recently emerged.
"Archaeology is a dangerous profession," says Estelle Lazer, a small, quietly spoken archaeologist from Sydney University.
"Nearly everyone who works in the field has exciting experiences, it's just the way the profession operates. There are either natural disasters or political problems," Lazer said.
DEATH VISITS THE JUNGLE

In late 1996, deep in the jungles of the Indonesian island of Aru, a tough five-day canoe and ferry trip to civilisation, Australian archaeologist Peter Veth lay motionless on a bed raised high above the ground on bamboo stilts.
Around him villagers, armed with bows and arrows, carried their freshly killed deer, while their hunting dogs followed hungrily.
Suffering from a potentially fatal cerebral malaria contracted from a mosquito bite, Veth fought a raging fever of 41 degrees Celsius (105 degrees Fahrenheit).
In the 1850s, British naturalist Alfred Wallace, who along with Charles Darwin developed the theory of natural selection, fought malaria for six weeks in the same jungle.
In 1987, a Japanese scientist on an Australian expedition to the Indonesian island of Sumba died of cerebral malaria.

Veth's companions decided to use a drug of last resort, despite the side effects of pyschosis and memory loss. Luckily for Veth, the drug broke his fever, although he did suffer memory loss for three months.

"It was surreal. I never had any real fear or worry. I just got weaker and weaker," Veth told Reuters. "I was still coherent and could talk to my colleagues and thought, well, if this is what it is like to die, then it's not too bad."
A few days later Veth was back inside a giant limestone cave searching for the first Australians -- those who migrated when Australia was attached to Asia some 30,000 to 60,000 years ago.
Veth's expedition was well prepared for the jungle's dangers, but in such a remote location, even a tiny mosquito can threaten death.
Veth will return to Aru next year.

"Archaeologists will try anything to get back to their site," says archaeologist Karin Sowada. "Often universities or funding organisations pull the plug because they don't want to be responsible for sending a team into a dangerous area."
MACHO MYTHS AND CURSES
The image of the adventurous scientists cheating death to bring back the treasures of antiquity has historically attracted Hollywood and stirred the hearts of archaeologists.

On a bright November day in 1922 English archaeologist Howard Carter made one of the world's greatest discoveries when he broke his way into the treasure-stacked tomb of King Tutankhamun in Egypt's Valley of the Kings.
The subsequent death of Carter and two of his companions sparked the legendary curse of the Pharaohs and a series of Hollywood B-grade movies.
Earlier this month, Australian archaeologist Peter Matthews and his expedition were ambushed in a Mexican rain forest by up to 80 Mayan Indians armed with machetes, sticks and firearms.
Matthews, who was trying to retrieve a 1,300-year-old Mayan altar, threw himself into a roaring jungle river to escape the attack.
"I think a lot of people don't admit it in public, but they like the image of Indiana Jones. They think it is very romantic," explains Lazer.

"It makes rather good dinner conversation to tell people about your exploits," says Lazer, who has searched for icebergs while tied to the mast of a yacht in a force 10 gale and been chased by amorous male fur seals in Antarctica.

Lazer said many archaeologists had led Indiana Jones-style lives, hanging upside down over cliffs to read ancient texts or worked as spies because they could gain easy access to countries and had multi-lingual skills.
POLITICS, GRAVE ROBBERS AND CHAUVINISTS
Sowada, assistant curator of Sydney University's Nicholson Museum of Antiquity, knows only too well the dangers faced by archaeologists -- especially women.
During a 1994 dig in the Middle East, Sowada and her team spent their nights trapped in a house as police and grave robbers engaged in gun battles.
"Grave robbers are a problem. It is not unusual for a site to be vandalised overnight because locals have got wind of a discovery or even the rumour of a discovery," Sowada said.
The shifting sands of Middle East politics constantly create a dangerous environment for archaeologist, but the more omnipresent danger for women archaeologists is sexual politics.

"In the Middle East a lot of men are not used to women in positions of authority," Sowada said. "Many men have a distorted perception of Western women -- that they are promiscuous and dress in provocative fashions.
"Some women invent imaginary husbands and families to help them in the field."
